stem_html:
The choreographer's instructions to the dancers are deliberately ______: she names a quality the movement should have and refuses to say which joint should produce it.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"severe","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"improvised","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"underspecified"},{"letter":"D","content":"contradictory","trap":"too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The colon says what she does and what she declines to do.
  • Incomplete is not the same as inconsistent.
  • Ask whose behaviour the blank describes.

Why A is wrong Severe is about the tone of the instruction, and the colon describes its content.

Why B is wrong The improvising is the dancers'; the instruction itself is written and deliberate.

Why C is right She supplies one thing and withholds another: she “names a quality the movement should have and refuses to say which joint” delivers it. An instruction that leaves the means open is underspecified.

Why D is wrong Contradictory would require two instructions that cannot both be followed. She gives one, incompletely.

stem_html:
The two accounts of the strike are not opposed so much as ______: the union's records begin on the morning the mill closed, and the owner's end the night before.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"identical","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"B","content":"unreliable","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"competing","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"complementary"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Not X so much as Y” needs Y to differ from X.
  • Adjoining is neither overlapping nor conflicting.
  • One choice restates the word the sentence rejects.

Why A is wrong Identical accounts would cover the same ground, and these cover adjoining ground.

Why B is wrong Nothing questions the accuracy of either record; the colon describes their coverage.

Why C is wrong Competing is a near-synonym for opposed, which the sentence has just ruled out.

Why D is right One record stops where the other starts — “the union's records begin on the morning the mill closed, and the owner's end the night before” — so together they cover the whole and neither overlaps the other. That is complementarity.

stem_html:
The reforms proved ______ in a way their authors had not intended: each measure worked as designed, and the four of them together produced a delay longer than the one they were meant to remove.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "self-defeating"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "ineffective", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "unpopular", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "ambitious", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Every part succeeding and the whole failing is the shape.
  • Failing to work and working against yourself are different.
  • The blank must describe the outcome.

Why A is right Every measure worked and the aggregate reversed the goal, so the reforms defeated themselves by succeeding. That is what “each measure worked as designed” makes precise.

Why B is wrong Ineffective would mean the measures did not work, and the sentence says each one did.

Why C is wrong Public reaction is never mentioned.

Why D is wrong Ambition describes the aim rather than the outcome the sentence reports.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2017 article about weather records.

The longest continuous rainfall record in the country was kept not by a government office but by four generations of one family, who measured the gauge in their yard at seven each morning for a hundred and twelve years. Meteorologists were slow to use it, since it had no official standing. They use it now for the reason they once ignored it: nobody changed the instrument, the site, or the hour.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"To argue that official weather stations should be run by families.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"B","content":"To explain how the feature that once disqualified a record turned out to be what made it valuable."},{"letter":"C","content":"To criticize meteorologists for neglecting amateur observations.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"To describe the daily routine that produced a long rainfall record.","trap":"half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Purpose is the turn, not the topic.
  • The final sentence names the reversal outright.
  • Reported delay is not stated criticism.

Why A is wrong No such recommendation appears.

Why B is right The last sentence turns the objection into the reason: they use it now “for the reason they once ignored it”, which is the unbroken method.

Why C is wrong The delay is reported without blame, and criticism is not the point the text builds to.

Why D is wrong The routine is the evidence for the reversal rather than the purpose.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2016 essay on museum lighting.

Curators speak of light as a debt. A watercolour can be shown for so many hours in its life and no more, and every exhibition draws on an account that is never replenished. The question is therefore not whether to darken a gallery but whom to darken it for, since the visitor kept in the dark today is the reason a visitor in 2200 will see anything at all.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"It introduces a second constraint that the text goes on to weigh against the first.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"It restates the metaphor of the debt in nontechnical language.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"It converts the technical constraint described earlier into a question about competing audiences, which the rest of the sentence answers."},{"letter":"D","content":"It concedes that darkening galleries is unpopular with visitors.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Ask what changes between the sentence before and the sentence after.
  • “Not whether but whom” is a reframing.
  • Restating and reframing are different jobs.

Why A is wrong No second constraint appears; the same one is restated as a choice.

Why B is wrong It does more than restate: it changes the subject of the question from whether to whom.

Why C is right The preceding sentences set up a fixed budget of hours; the underlined clause makes it a choice — “not whether to darken a gallery but whom to darken it for” — between today's visitor and a visitor in 2200, which the closing clause then settles.

Why D is wrong Popularity is never raised.

stem_html:
Text 1

Requiring code to be published alongside a paper has raised the quality of computational research. Since the policy took effect, the proportion of results in this journal that an independent group can reproduce has risen from about a third to nearly three-quarters.

Text 2

The rise is real, but the policy did not cause all of it. Groups that were unable or unwilling to release code stopped submitting here, and their papers now appear elsewhere. A journal that has changed which studies it receives cannot read its own reproducibility rate as a measure of how much research improved.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely characterize the increase reported in Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"As a fabrication produced by selective reporting of reproducibility tests.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"B","content":"As proof that mandatory code release should be adopted by every journal.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"C","content":"As too small to establish that the policy had any effect.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"D","content":"As partly an effect of a change in which studies the journal receives rather than of better practice alone."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Selection effects concede the number and dispute the cause.
  • “The rise is real” rules out the fraud reading.
  • Partly is the word to look for.

Why A is wrong Text 2 opens by saying the rise is real, so it charges no fabrication.

Why B is wrong That is Text 1's conclusion, not Text 2's.

Why C is wrong Text 2 never disputes the size of the increase, only what it measures.

Why D is right Text 2 grants the rise and reassigns part of it: “groups that were unable or unwilling to release code stopped submitting here”, so the pool changed as well as the practice.

stem_html: An economist argued that a city's new bus lane reduced car journey times on parallel streets because it removed buses from the general traffic, not because it reduced the total number of cars. Which finding, if true, would most directly support the economist's argument?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Car counts on the parallel streets were unchanged after the lane opened, while the number of times a car had to stop behind a bus fell by four-fifths."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Average car journey times on the parallel streets fell by three minutes after the lane opened.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Bus ridership rose by 12 percent in the year after the lane opened.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Car counts on the parallel streets fell by a fifth after the lane opened.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Because X, not because Y” needs Y held constant.
  • Confirming the effect is not identifying the cause.
  • The rejected mechanism is always offered as a choice.

Why A is right The argument is that the lane worked “because it removed buses from the general traffic, not because it reduced the total number of cars”, so the finding has to hold car numbers steady while the bus interaction changes. Unchanged counts with stops behind buses down four-fifths does exactly that.

Why B is wrong This confirms the effect and says nothing about which mechanism produced it.

Why C is wrong Ridership is about buses, and the claim is about what happened to cars.

Why D is wrong Fewer cars is the rival explanation the economist rejects.

stem_html: A paleontologist claimed that a set of fossil trackways was made by a single animal walking in a circle rather than by several animals walking in a line. Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the claim?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"No other trackways of the same age occur at the site.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"Every print in the sequence shows the same healed fracture in the third toe, and the depth of the prints changes gradually and continuously around the circle."},{"letter":"C","content":"The prints are all the same size and shape.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"The trackway forms a closed loop about nine metres across.","trap":"half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Look for the feature that is individual, not typical.
  • A pathology is a signature; a shape is not.
  • Both hypotheses predict a loop.

Why A is wrong The absence of other trackways says nothing about how this one was made.

Why B is right The claim is that the trackways were made “by a single animal walking in a circle rather than by several animals”, and a healed fracture is individual, so a print carrying it at every step must come from one animal. Continuously changing depth rules out separate animals arriving at intervals.

Why C is wrong Animals of one species leave prints of the same size and shape, so this fits both explanations.

Why D is wrong A line of animals following one another can also trace a loop.

stem_html:
Researchers measured how accurately listeners identified the emotion in short speech clips played in four conditions. They concluded that removing the words while keeping the melody of the voice cost listeners very little, whereas removing the melody while keeping the words cost them a great deal.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researchers' conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Accuracy with only the words remaining was 46%, well above the 27% obtained when neither cue remained.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"B","content":"Accuracy with only the melody remaining was 79%, the second-highest value in the graph.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"Accuracy fell from 84% with full speech to 79% when only the melody remained, but to 46% when only the words remained."},{"letter":"D","content":"Accuracy was highest with full speech and lowest when neither cue remained.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two losses means two subtractions from one baseline.
  • Comparing to the floor answers a different question.
  • A rank is not a magnitude.

Why A is wrong This compares the words condition with the floor rather than with full speech.

Why B is wrong One value with a rank is not a comparison of the two losses.

Why C is right The conclusion is that “removing the words while keeping the melody of the voice cost listeners very little” while the reverse cost a great deal, so it compares two losses against the same baseline. Only this choice gives both: 5 points lost when the words go, 38 when the melody goes.

Why D is wrong The two extremes are consistent with any ordering of the middle two conditions.

stem_html: In his memoir Downriver, Teodoro Vasquez describes his father's silence not as an absence of speech but as a form of instruction the son only recognized years later. Which quotation from a fictional memoir would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"“My father rarely spoke, and when he did it was about the weather or the engine.”","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"“He taught me the names of every tree on the river, patiently, one afternoon at a time.”","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"C","content":"“His silence hurt me then and it hurts me now, and I have never found the use in it.”","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"“He would not name the tree for me. He stood there until I had walked round it twice, and it is thirty years before I understood that this was the lesson and not the withholding of one.”"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The claim has two halves: instruction, and delayed recognition.
  • A quotation that reports the silence without meaning fails the first half.
  • Explicit denial of the claim is a common distractor.

Why A is wrong This reports the silence as a habit and finds no instruction in it.

Why B is wrong Here the father teaches by speaking, which is the opposite of the claim.

Why C is wrong This narrator explicitly denies ever finding a use in the silence.

Why D is right The claim is that the silence was “a form of instruction the son only recognized years later”. Here it is deliberate and pedagogical — he waits while the son circles the tree — and the recognition is explicitly delayed by thirty years.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2022 article about seed banks.

A seed bank stores what a crop is at the moment of storage. A field, by contrast, stores what a crop is becoming: the varieties farmers keep planting change every season in response to the pests and weather of that season. A bank protects a variety from extinction and, at the same time, stops it adapting. Both kinds of conservation are necessary, and neither can substitute for the other.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Storing seed and continuing to grow a crop preserve different things, so both are needed."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Seed banks are the most reliable way of protecting crop varieties from extinction.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Farmers change the varieties they plant in response to pests and weather.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Crops kept in seed banks eventually lose the ability to adapt to new conditions.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A both/neither sentence is usually the main idea.
  • A contrast asks for an answer that keeps both sides.
  • Halting adaptation is not destroying the capacity for it.

Why A is right The passage contrasts the two and closes on the claim that “both kinds of conservation are necessary, and neither can substitute for the other”.

Why B is wrong Reliability is not compared, and the text's point is that banking alone is not enough.

Why C is wrong This is a supporting detail about fields.

Why D is wrong The text says a bank stops a variety adapting while stored, not that the variety loses a capacity.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2015 essay on maps.

The surveyors who made the first accurate map of the delta worked for eleven years and produced a document that was obsolete on the day it was printed. Channels there move faster than surveyors can walk. What the map preserved was not the delta but the surveyors' route through it, and that route is now the only record of villages the river has since taken.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Rivers destroy villages faster than mapmakers can record them.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"B","content":"A map that failed at its intended purpose became valuable as a record of something else."},{"letter":"C","content":"Surveying a delta accurately is impossible because its channels move.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"The surveyors spent eleven years on a document that was never used.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Failure plus unexpected value is the shape.
  • The setup is not the point.
  • The last sentence carries the second value.

Why A is wrong This turns a detail about the villages into the main claim.

Why B is right The map is obsolete as a map, and the closing sentence gives it a second value: the route is “the only record of villages the river has since taken”.

Why C is wrong The difficulty is the setup, not the point the text arrives at.

Why D is wrong The text says the opposite of never used — the record is used now.

stem_html:
Two identical batches of a fermented sauce were left in cellars of the same temperature and humidity, one in a building of stone and one of timber. After nine months the timber-cellar batch carried three yeast species absent from the stone batch, and those three were the species found on the timber itself. Since the ingredients and the conditions were the same, the difference in the finished sauce ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"indicates that the two batches were not in fact identical at the start.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"B","content":"means temperature has no effect on fermentation.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"C","content":"is most plausibly explained by organisms the building itself contributed."},{"letter":"D","content":"shows that timber cellars produce better sauce than stone ones.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • What varied is the only candidate cause.
  • The matching species name the source.
  • A held-constant variable is untested, not disproved.

Why A is wrong The passage states the batches were identical, so this contradicts the premise rather than following from it.

Why B is wrong Holding temperature constant shows nothing about what temperature does.

Why C is right The controlled variables cannot explain a difference, and the three extra species “were the species found on the timber itself”, which points at the building as the source.

Why D is wrong Quality is never assessed; only composition differs.

stem_html:
A publisher offered readers a choice between a printed newsletter and an email version. Subscriptions to the printed version fell by half over three years while total subscriptions rose by a fifth, and surveys found that readers who switched cited delivery speed rather than cost, which was the same for both. This suggests that the decline in printed subscriptions ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"was caused by the higher price of the printed version.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"B","content":"will continue until the printed version is discontinued.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"shows that readers prefer shorter newsletters.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"D","content":"reflects readers moving between formats rather than losing interest in the newsletter."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A falling part inside a rising whole is a shift.
  • Check the choice against the stated reason.
  • An inference is not a forecast.

Why A is wrong The passage says cost “was the same for both”.

Why B is wrong A prediction requires evidence about the future that the passage does not give.

Why C is wrong Length is never mentioned; the two versions carry the same newsletter.

Why D is right Total subscriptions rose while print fell, so readers stayed with the publication and changed format — and they “cited delivery speed rather than cost” for doing so.

stem_html:
The bridge was designed to carry a tram that was never built ______ its deck is twice as wide as the traffic it now takes requires.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "; as a result,"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", as a result,", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": " as a result,", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ", as a result", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • However, therefore, as a result — adverbs, not conjunctions.
  • Semicolon before, comma after.
  • Two independent clauses need more than a comma.

Why A is right Two independent clauses joined by a conjunctive adverb take a semicolon before the adverb and a comma after it.

Why B is wrong As a result is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so a comma in front of it leaves a splice.

Why C is wrong With no mark at all before the adverb the two clauses run together.

Why D is wrong The punctuation is on the wrong side and the splice remains.

stem_html:
The lens that the observatory ground in 1897 ______ still the largest refracting lens ever put into regular service, weighs half a tonne.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":" —","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"B","content":","},{"letter":"C","content":" and","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"D","content":";","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Find the closing mark before choosing the opening one.
  • An appositive interrupts; it does not coordinate.
  • Match dashes with dashes and commas with commas.

Why A is wrong A dash cannot be closed by a comma; enclosing marks must match, and the closing mark is already a comma.

Why B is right The phrase is an appositive interrupting subject from verb, and it is already closed by a comma before weighs, so it has to be opened by one.

Why C is wrong And would make the phrase a second element of a compound, but there is nothing for it to be compounded with.

Why D is wrong A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and neither side here is one.

stem_html:
Although the recipe calls for a full day of resting ______ dough left overnight in a cold kitchen behaves almost identically.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":" a","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"B","content":": a","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":", a"},{"letter":"D","content":"; a","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Although, because, while, since — all subordinate.
  • Dependent clause first, then a comma.

Why B is wrong A colon has the same requirement a semicolon does.

stem_html:
The expedition sent back three reports ______ one from the base camp, one from the col, and one written on the summit ridge and never signed.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":",","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"B","content":";","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"C","content":" and","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":":"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A colon needs a complete sentence in front and an explanation after.
  • The list renames the noun the first half ends on.
  • A semicolon needs a sentence on both sides.

Why B is wrong A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a list of three noun phrases is not one.

Why D is right The first half is a complete sentence and the second half itemizes the three reports it ends on, which is what a colon announces.

stem_html:
The number of applications the office received in March ______ larger than the total for the whole of the previous year.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "was"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "were", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "have been", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "are", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}]

  • Strike the of-phrase and reread.

stem_html:
Cast in one piece in 1642 and never recast, ______ a semitone flat for the whole of its working life.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"what the tower held was a bell ringing","trap":"modifier-attachment"},{"letter":"B","content":"the bell rang"},{"letter":"C","content":"the ringers lived with a bell that rang","trap":"modifier-attachment"},{"letter":"D","content":"there was a bell in the tower that rang","trap":"modifier-attachment"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The noun right after the comma is the one being described. Read the opening phrase and ask what it is true of.
  • A choice can name the bell and still fail. What matters is whether the bell is the subject, not whether the word appears.
  • “There was” and “what the tower held” both bury the subject.

Why A is wrong “What the tower held” is a clause, not the bell itself, and it is that clause the modifier would be describing.

Why B is right The opening phrase describes something cast in 1642 and never recast, and that is the bell. Putting “the bell” directly after the comma is what makes the modifier land on the thing it describes.

Why C is wrong The ringers were not cast in one piece in 1642. The phrase attaches to the first noun after the comma, and here that is the wrong one.

Why D is wrong “There” is not something that can be cast, so the modifier has nothing to attach to.

stem_html:
By the time the auditor arrived in March, the shop ______ its stock twice, and neither count agreed with the ledger.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"counts","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"B","content":"was counting","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"C","content":"had counted"},{"letter":"D","content":"has counted","trap":"distant-antecedent"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “By the time” sets up two past events. The earlier one takes the past perfect.
  • The present perfect reaches to now, and this sentence never comes back to now.
  • Twice, and both compared — the counting is finished, not in progress.

Why A is wrong The present tense puts the counting in the present, which contradicts “by the time the auditor arrived”.

Why B is wrong The past progressive would have the counting still going on when the auditor arrived, but the sentence says both counts were done and compared.

Why C is right Both counts were finished before the auditor arrived, and the arrival is itself in the past. The past perfect is what places one past event before another.

Why D is wrong The present perfect ties the counting to now. The sentence has already fixed its reference point in March.

stem_html:
The two mills each produced their own flour, and ______ was milled more finely than the other's.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"the older mills","trap":"pronoun-ambiguity"},{"letter":"B","content":"the older mills'","trap":"pronoun-ambiguity"},{"letter":"C","content":"the older mill","trap":"pronoun-ambiguity"},{"letter":"D","content":"the older mill's"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Comparisons must match in kind.
  • The other's is possessive, so its partner must be too.
  • Check whether the apostrophe is before or after the s.

Why A is wrong A plural noun, where the sentence needs one mill's flour.

Why B is wrong A plural possessive, which cannot refer to a single mill.

Why C is wrong This compares a mill with a flour rather than two flours.

Why D is right The comparison is between two flours, and the other's is possessive, so the first term has to be the possessive the older mill's standing for its flour.

stem_html:
Restoring the wetland was expected to take a decade of planting and pumping. ______ the engineers removed one culvert, and the marsh reflooded itself in a winter.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

Why B is wrong Consequently would make the single culvert a result of the decade-long expectation.

Traps in this question

  • Evidence then conclusion is a consequence.
  • Two detectors is the reason, so the transition is causal.
  • Contrast words need two sides that disagree.

Why A is wrong There is no contrast between the evidence and the conclusion drawn from it.

Why B is right The second sentence is the conclusion the first supports: independent replication is precisely what rules out a single-instrument artifact.

Why C is wrong Nevertheless marks a contrast, and the two sentences agree.

Why D is wrong The second sentence is an inference, not an instance of the first.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Phoenix Islands Protected Area was closed to commercial fishing in 2015.
  • It covers about 408,000 square kilometres of the central Pacific.
  • Kiribati reopened part of the area to licensed fishing in 2021.
  • Coral cover inside the closed area recovered from 2010 bleaching by 2018.
  • Reefs outside the area with the same bleaching history did not recover.

The student wants to present evidence that the closure had an effect. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Evidence of an effect is a comparison. One side of it is not enough.
  • The strongest-sounding single fact is the incomplete one. Choice B is true and proves nothing.
  • Dates and dimensions are not outcomes.

Why A is wrong This is the history of the designation. It reports no outcome at all.

Why B is wrong Recovery inside the area on its own is consistent with the bleaching simply passing. Without the reefs outside, there is nothing to attribute it to.

Why C is right Evidence of an effect needs a comparison, and this is the only choice that supplies one: the same bleaching, inside and outside, with different outcomes.

Why D is wrong The size of the area is a fact about it, not evidence that closing it changed anything.
